title: Book III: Waiting For Death — Chapter XXIV
paragraphs:
“The wrongdoer's sorrow offers little comfort
To the one who carries the burden of the wrong.”
—SHAKESPEARE, Sonnets.

I am sorry to report that just three days after the promising events at Houndsley, Fred Vincy was more dejected than he had ever been. The expected buyer for his horse had not failed him. Rather, before the sale to Lord Medlicote's man could be completed, Diamond, in whom eighty pounds' worth of hope had been invested, suddenly displayed a vicious passion for kicking in the stable. He narrowly missed killing the groom and finally caught a leg in a rope hanging over the stall partition, badly laming himself. Fred had no more remedy than someone who discovers a spouse's bad temper after marriage, a temper old acquaintances naturally knew beforehand. For some reason he showed none of his usual resilience under this misfortune. He knew only that he had fifty pounds, no prospect of getting more at present, and a bill for a hundred and sixty due in five days. Even if he appealed to his father to spare Mr. Garth a loss, Fred felt painfully certain of the response. His father would angrily refuse to rescue Garth from the consequences of what he would call encouraging extravagance and deceit. Fred was so utterly cast down that he could think of nothing but going straight to Mr. Garth with the truth, taking the fifty pounds and at least getting that safely out of his own hands. His father was at the warehouse and did not yet know of the accident. Once told, he would rage about the vicious animal being brought into his stable. Before facing that lesser trouble, Fred wanted to leave with all his courage intact for the greater one. He took his father's horse, having decided that after Mr. Garth he would ride to Stone Court and confess everything to Mary. Indeed, without Mary and his love for her, his conscience would probably have been much less active, both in bringing the debt continually to mind and in urging him now not to spare himself in his usual way by postponing an unpleasant task, but to act as directly and simply as possible. Even people far stronger than Fred Vincy keep half their honesty in the mind of the person they love most. “The theater of all my actions has fallen,” said an ancient figure when his closest friend died. Those whose audience demands their best are fortunate in their theater. At that time it would certainly have made a considerable difference to Fred if Mary Garth had held no firm ideas about admirable character.

Mr. Garth was not at his office, so Fred rode to the house a little outside town: a plain, rambling, old-fashioned timber-framed building with an orchard in front. It had been a farmhouse before the town expanded; now private gardens surrounded it. We grow fonder of houses when they have faces of their own, like friends. The large Garth family—Mary had four brothers and a sister—loved the old house, although its best furniture had long since been sold. Fred loved it too. He knew every part, even the attic with its delicious smell of apples and quinces. Until today he had never approached it without pleasant expectations. Now his heart beat uneasily at the likelihood of having to confess before Mrs. Garth, whom he feared rather more than her husband. She was not prone to sarcasm and impulsive remarks as Mary was. At least in her present, matronly years she never committed herself by speaking hastily. As she said, she had borne the yoke in youth and learned self-control. She had the rare good sense to recognize what could not be changed and submit without complaint. Adoring her husband's virtues, she had accepted early his inability to protect his own interests and had faced the consequences cheerfully. She was generous enough to surrender all pride in teapots or children's frills. She never confided mournfully to neighboring women about Mr. Garth's imprudence and how much money he might have had if only he resembled other men. Those neighbors consequently considered her proud or eccentric and sometimes spoke to their husbands of “your fine Mrs. Garth.” She criticized them in return, being better educated than most Middlemarch matrons and—where is the faultless woman?—inclined to severity towards her own sex, which she believed intended for complete subordination. Men's failings, on the other hand, received disproportionate indulgence; she often called them natural. It must also be admitted that she resisted what she considered foolishness a little too emphatically. The move from governess to housewife had impressed itself too deeply on her self-awareness. She seldom forgot that, although her grammar and accent surpassed local standards, she wore a plain cap, cooked the family dinner, and darned every stocking. Sometimes she taught pupils as she moved around, having them follow her through the kitchen with books or slates. She thought it wholesome for them to see her making excellent soapsuds while correcting their mistakes without looking: to know that a woman with sleeves above her elbows could understand the subjunctive mood or the tropical zone. In short, a woman could possess “education” and other admirable things ending in “tion,” worthy of emphatic pronunciation, without being a useless doll. Delivering such improving observations, she wore a firm little frown that did not prevent her face from looking kind. Her words marched out in procession in a warm, pleasant contralto. Certainly the exemplary Mrs. Garth had comic aspects, but her character supported her peculiarities as a very fine wine supports a taste of the skin.

She felt motherly towards Fred and had always excused his mistakes, though she would probably not have forgiven Mary for becoming engaged to him. Her daughter came under the stricter judgment she applied to women. The very unusualness of her indulgence made it harder for Fred to know he must now fall in her estimation. His visit proved still more uncomfortable than expected. Caleb had gone out early to inspect repairs nearby. At certain hours Mrs. Garth was always in the kitchen, and that morning she was managing several tasks at once. She made pies at a well-scrubbed pine table along one side of the airy room, watched Sally at the oven and dough tub through an open door, and taught her youngest boy and girl, who stood opposite with books and slates. A tub and drying rack at the other end showed that small items of washing were being dealt with between times.

Mrs. Garth, sleeves rolled above the elbows, deftly rolling pastry and pinching decorative edges while explaining with grammatical fervor how verbs and pronouns should agree with “collective nouns, or words signifying many,” was a pleasantly amusing sight. Like Mary, she had curly hair and a square face, but she was handsomer, with finer features, pale skin, a solid matronly figure, and a remarkably steady gaze. In her cap with its snowy frill, she recalled that delightful Frenchwoman we have all seen shopping with a basket on her arm. Looking at the mother, one could hope the daughter would grow like her, a future advantage equal to a dowry. Too often a mother stands behind her daughter like a threatening prophecy: “What I am, she will soon be.”

“Now, once more,” said Mrs. Garth, pinching an apple pastry that appeared to distract Ben, an energetic boy with a heavy brow, from the lesson. “‘With attention to whether the word conveys an idea of unity or plurality.’ Tell me again what that means, Ben.”
Like more celebrated educators, Mrs. Garth favored certain old paths. In a general shipwreck of society, she would have tried to hold her Lindley Murray grammar above the waves.
“Oh, it means you have to think what you mean,” Ben replied peevishly. “I hate grammar. What's it for?”
“To teach you to speak and write correctly so people can understand you,” Mrs. Garth said with stern precision. “Would you like to speak like old Job?”
“Yes,” Ben answered firmly. “It's funnier. He says ‘Yo goo.’ That's as good as ‘You go.’”
“But he says ‘There's a ship in the garden’ instead of ‘a sheep,’” Letty said with superiority. “You might think he meant a ship from the sea.”
“Not unless you were silly,” Ben said. “How would a ship from the sea get there?”

“That's only pronunciation, the smallest part of grammar,” said Mrs. Garth. “That apple peel is for the pigs, Ben. If you eat it, I'll have to give them your slice of pie. Job only has to discuss very simple matters. How would you speak or write about anything difficult if you knew as little grammar as he does? You'd choose the wrong words and put them in the wrong places. Instead of understanding you, people would turn away because you were tiresome. What would you do then?”
“I wouldn't care. I'd stop,” said Ben, feeling this a pleasant way out where grammar was concerned.

“I see you're growing tired and foolish, Ben,” said his mother, accustomed to such obstructive reasoning from her sons. Having finished the pies, she moved towards the drying rack. “Come here and tell me Wednesday's story about Cincinnatus.”
“I know! He was a farmer,” Ben said.
“Ben, he was a Roman. Let ME tell it,” said Letty, pushing with her elbow.
“Silly, he was a Roman farmer, and he was plowing.”
“Yes, but something happened before that. It wasn't the beginning. People wanted him,” said Letty.
“First you have to say what sort of man he was,” Ben insisted. “He was wise, like father, so people wanted his advice. And brave, and able to fight. Father could fight too, couldn't he, mother?”
“Let me tell it straight through, Ben, the way mother did,” said Letty, frowning. “Mother, please tell Ben to be quiet.”

“Letty, I'm ashamed of you,” her mother said, wringing caps out of the tub. “Your brother began. You should have waited to see whether he could tell it. How rude you look, shoving and frowning as if you meant to conquer people with your elbows! I'm sure Cincinnatus would have been sorry to see his daughter behave like that.” She pronounced this terrible sentence with such majesty that Letty felt life already painful, between being forbidden to talk and being held in general disapproval, even by the Romans. “Now, Ben.”
“Well—oh—there was lots of fighting, and they were all blockheads, and—I can't tell it exactly as you did—but they needed someone to be captain and king and everything—”
“Dictator,” Letty interrupted with an injured look and some wish to make her mother sorry.
“All right, dictator!” Ben said scornfully. “But that's a bad word. He wasn't dictating things for them to write on slates.”
“Come, Ben, you know better than that,” Mrs. Garth said, carefully keeping a serious face. “Listen, someone's knocking. Run and open the door, Letty.”

It was Fred. When Letty said her father was still out but her mother was in the kitchen, he had no choice. He always went to see Mrs. Garth there if she was working, and could hardly change his habit now. Silently putting an arm round Letty's neck, he led her in without his usual jokes and affectionate gestures.
Mrs. Garth was surprised to see him so early, but she rarely expressed surprise. Continuing her work calmly, she merely said:
“You, Fred, at this hour? You're very pale. Has something happened?”

“I need to speak to Mr. Garth,” Fred said, not yet ready for more. After a pause he added, “And to you.” He assumed she knew all about the note. In the end he must mention it before her, if not to her alone.

“Caleb will be back in a few minutes,” said Mrs. Garth, imagining trouble between Fred and his father. “He can't be long. He has work at his desk that must be finished this morning. Would you mind staying with me while I finish here?”
“We don't have to go on with Cincinnatus, do we?” asked Ben, who had taken Fred's whip and was testing it on the cat.
“No, you may go out. But put down that whip. How cruel to whip poor old Tortoise! Please take it from him, Fred.”
“Come on, old fellow, hand it over,” Fred said, holding out his hand.
“Can I ride your horse today?” Ben asked, surrendering the whip with an air of doing so freely.
“Not today. Another time. This isn't my horse.”
“Will you see Mary today?”
“Yes, I think so,” said Fred, feeling an unpleasant pang.
“Tell her to come home soon, play forfeits, and make us laugh.”
“That's enough, Ben. Run along,” said Mrs. Garth, noticing Fred's discomfort.

“Are Letty and Ben your only pupils now?” Fred asked once they had gone and something was needed to pass the time. He still could not decide whether to wait for Caleb or seize an opening in the conversation to confess to Mrs. Garth, give her the money, and ride away.

“I have one other, just one. Fanny Hackbutt comes at half past eleven. I'm not earning much now,” Mrs. Garth said with a smile. “Pupils are scarce. But I've saved my little fund for Alfred's apprenticeship fee: ninety-two pounds. He can go to Mr. Hanmer now. He's just the right age.”

This was no promising introduction to the news that Mr. Garth was about to lose more than ninety-two pounds. Fred remained silent. “Young gentlemen at university cost rather more,” Mrs. Garth innocently continued, straightening the edging on a cap. “Caleb thinks Alfred will become a distinguished engineer. He wants to give the boy a good chance. There he is! I hear him. Shall we go to him in the parlor?”
When they entered, Caleb had put down his hat and seated himself at the desk.

“Why, Fred, my boy!” he said with mild surprise, holding his pen before dipping it. “You're here early.” Missing the customary cheerful greeting in Fred's face, he immediately added, “Trouble at home? Is something wrong?”

“Yes, Mr. Garth. I've come to tell you something I'm afraid will make you think badly of me. I have to tell you and Mrs. Garth that I can't keep my word. I can't find the money for the bill after all. I've had bad luck. I've only these fifty pounds towards the hundred and sixty.”

As he spoke, Fred took out the notes and placed them on the desk. He had blurted out the bare facts, miserable as a boy and unable to find helpful words. Mrs. Garth, silently astonished, looked to her husband for an explanation. Caleb blushed. After a short pause he said:
“Oh, Susan, I didn't tell you. I signed a bill for Fred, for a hundred and sixty pounds. He was certain he could pay it himself.”
Mrs. Garth's face plainly changed, but like a change beneath water whose surface stays smooth. Fixing her eyes on Fred, she said:
“I suppose you've asked your father for the rest and he's refused.”
“No,” Fred said, biting his lip and finding speech harder. “But I know asking would be useless. Unless it could help, I wouldn't want to bring Mr. Garth's name into it.”

“It's come at a bad time,” Caleb said hesitantly, looking at the notes and nervously fingering the paper. “Christmas here, and money rather tight. You see, I have to cut everything out like a tailor with too little cloth. What can we do, Susan? I'll need every penny in the bank. It's a hundred and ten pounds, damn it!”

“I must give you the ninety-two pounds I've saved for Alfred's apprenticeship,” said Mrs. Garth gravely and firmly, though a sensitive ear might have detected a slight tremor in some words. “And Mary must have saved twenty pounds from her salary by now. She will lend it.”

She had not looked at Fred again and was not calculating which words would wound him most. Eccentric woman that she was, she was absorbed in deciding what to do and did not imagine bitter comments or explosions would help. Yet for the first time she made Fred feel something like the bite of remorse. Strangely, his earlier distress had consisted almost entirely of knowing he must appear dishonorable and lose the Garths' respect. He had not dwelt on the inconvenience and possible harm his failure would cause them. Optimistic young gentlemen seldom exercise their imaginations on other people's needs. Indeed, most of us are raised to think that the highest reason for avoiding wrongdoing has nothing to do with those who would suffer it. But now Fred suddenly saw himself as a contemptible scoundrel robbing two women of their savings.
“I'll certainly repay everything, Mrs. Garth—eventually,” he stammered.

“Yes, eventually,” she replied. Having a particular dislike of fine words on ugly occasions, she could not resist one sharp saying. “But boys can't conveniently be apprenticed eventually. They need to be apprenticed at fifteen.” Never had she felt less inclined to excuse Fred.

“The greater fault was mine, Susan,” said Caleb. “Fred felt certain he'd find the money. But I had no business putting my hand to bills. You've looked everywhere and tried every honest means, I suppose?” he added, turning his compassionate gray eyes on Fred. He was too tactful to name Mr. Featherstone.

“Yes, I've tried everything. I really have. I'd have had a hundred and thirty pounds but for an accident with a horse I was about to sell. My uncle had given me eighty. I traded my old horse and thirty pounds for another that I meant to sell for eighty or more. I intended to do without a horse. But it's turned out vicious and lamed itself. I wish I'd gone to the devil, horses and all, before bringing this on you. Nobody matters more to me. You and Mrs. Garth have always been so kind. But saying that is useless. You'll always think me a scoundrel now.”
Fred turned and hurried from the room, aware of becoming rather tearful and vaguely feeling that his sorrow did the Garths little good. They watched him mount and ride quickly through the gate.

“Fred Vincy disappoints me,” said Mrs. Garth. “I would never have believed he'd involve you in his debts. I knew he was extravagant, but not that he'd be mean enough to put his risks on his oldest friend, the person least able to afford a loss.”
“I was a fool, Susan.”

“You were,” his wife said, nodding and smiling. “But I wouldn't have announced it in the marketplace. Why keep such things from me? It's the same with your buttons. You let them come off without telling me and go out with your cuff dangling. If I'd known, I might have had a better plan ready.”
“I know you're deeply upset, Susan,” Caleb said, looking at her tenderly. “I can't bear your losing the money you've scraped together for Alfred.”

“It's fortunate I HAD scraped it together. And you'll be the one to suffer, because you'll have to teach the boy yourself. You must give up your bad habits. Some men take to drink; you've taken to working for nothing. You must indulge yourself less in that. And you must ride over to Mary and ask what money she has.”
Caleb had pushed his chair back. He leaned forward, slowly shaking his head and carefully fitting his fingertips together.
“Poor Mary!” he said. Then, more quietly, “Susan, I'm afraid she may love Fred.”
“Oh no. She's always laughing at him. And he's unlikely to think of her as anything but a sister.”
Caleb did not answer. Presently he lowered his spectacles, pulled his chair up to the desk, and said, “Damn the bill! I wish it were in Hanover. These things interrupt business terribly.”

The first part exhausted his vocabulary of curses and came out in a slight snarl, easy enough to imagine. But anyone who had never heard him say “business” could scarcely understand the special fervent reverence, almost religious devotion, in which he wrapped that word, as a sacred object is wrapped in gold-fringed linen.

Caleb Garth often shook his head while contemplating the value and indispensable power of the labor, with its countless heads and hands, that feeds, clothes, and houses society. It had captured his imagination in boyhood. The ringing of great hammers building roofs or ships' keels, workers' shouted signals, the furnace's roar, the engine's thunder and splash—all were sublime music to him. Timber felled and loaded, a huge trunk trembling star-like far down the road, a crane working on the wharf, produce stacked in warehouses, the precision and variety of muscular effort wherever exact work was required: these youthful sights had given him poetry without poets, a philosophy without philosophers, a religion without theology. His early ambition was to take the most effective possible part in this magnificent labor, which he dignified in his own special way as “business.” Though briefly trained by a surveyor and otherwise largely self-taught, he knew more about land, building, and mining than most specialists in the county.

His division of human occupations was rather rough. Like the classifications of more famous men, it would not satisfy these advanced times. He divided them into “business, politics, preaching, learning, and amusement.” He had nothing against the last four, but regarded them as a reverent pagan regards gods other than his own. Similarly, he respected every social rank, yet would not have wanted to belong to one that prevented sufficiently close contact with business to earn the honorable marks of dust and mortar, engine moisture, or the sweet soil of woods and fields. He always considered himself an orthodox Christian and would discuss grace preceding human action if the subject arose. Nevertheless, I think his real gods were sound practical plans, accurate work, and faithful completion of a task. His prince of darkness was a careless worker. Caleb had no spirit of rejection in him, however. The world seemed so marvelous that he would accept any number of systems, like any number of heavens, provided they did not plainly obstruct good drainage, solid building, correct measurement, and sensible drilling for coal. He possessed, in fact, a reverent soul and strong practical intelligence. But he could not handle finance. He understood values, yet lacked the sharp imagination that calculates monetary profit and loss. Having learned this at a cost, he resolved to abandon every branch of his beloved business requiring that talent. He devoted himself entirely to the many kinds of work he could do without managing capital. Within his district he became one of those precious men everyone wants to employ: he worked well, charged little, and often refused payment altogether. No wonder the Garths were poor and lived modestly. They did not mind, however.
